title: Formal occasions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE FORMULA IS THE WHOLE OF IT. Samga goin-ui myeongbog-eul bimnida is said at every Korean funeral, word for word. A condolence a speaker builds themselves is wrong even when every word in it is right.

ENGLISH CONDOLENCE IS IMPROVISED AND THE VARIATION IS THE SINCERITY. Korean condolence is recited, and the sincerity is in saying it correctly, once, and briefly. An English-shaped improvisation reads as a stranger talking too much.
AN ENGLISH TOAST IS A SPEECH AND A KOREAN TOAST IS A WORD. Geonbae, or a noun plus wihayeo, and then everybody drinks. Anything longer has stopped being a toast and become a speech.

-(SEU)PNIDA IS PRODUCED HERE, NOT MERELY HEARD. L4-M7 taught the deferential register as something spoken at you, at the station and on the intercom. On these occasions you say it yourself, and the grammar is L4-M7's unchanged.

N-EUL/REUL WIHAYEO IS THE ONE PRODUCTIVE FRAME THE LEVEL CAN AFFORD. For the sake of: the noun takes its ordinary object particle and wihayeo follows it. It is the toast's own shape and the spine of any short occasion speech.

CHUKHAHAMNIDA DOES NOT STRETCH THE WAY CONGRATULATIONS DOES. It wants its occasion named in front of it — a marriage, a birthday, a graduation — and standing alone it is thinner in Korean than the English word is.
JUSIPSIO IS L1-M3'S JUSEYO IN THE DEFERENTIAL REGISTER. juseyo asks a person; jusipsio asks a room. Nothing else about the request changes, and the verb in front of it is unaffected.

THE NEW YEAR GREETING IS RECEIVED, NOT WISHED. Saehae bok mani badeuseyo says receive much luck, where English wishes it to you. The verb belongs to the listener — and mani and badeuseyo are already L2-M5's, so the greeting costs two words.

words.note: The occasion, and the noun chukhahamnida wants in front of it. It covers both the ceremony and the state that follows.
The congratulation, in the register an occasion asks for. Name the occasion in front of it: on its own it is thinner than the English word.

sentences.trap: English congratulations can stand alone at anything at all. chukhahamnida wants the occasion said first, and a bare one at a wedding sounds as though you had forgotten why you came.

variations.changed: a different occasion, and this one is fixed without the particle
the -yo register, for a friend rather than a room

mistake.why: Grammatical, and thin. Without gyeolhon-eul in front of it the congratulation names nothing, and at a wedding that is what it sounds like.

sentences.usage: At the reception desk of a wedding hall, to the family.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the occasion, then congratulate it.

words.note: The whole toast in one word. It is shouted, everybody answers it, and then everybody drinks — there is no speech attached.
Follows a noun carrying -eul or -reul. It is the toast's own shape, and the frame any short occasion speech is built on.

sentences.trap: An English toast is a paragraph and this is the whole of the Korean one. Adding sentences to it does not make it warmer; it makes it a speech nobody asked for.

variations.changed: the toast with nothing named
a pronoun in the frame instead of the occasion

mistake.why: wihayeo needs the object particle on the noun in front of it. Without -eul the frame has nothing to hold, and the toast comes out as two nouns side by side.

sentences.usage: Glass raised, at the table, once.
sentences.mnemonic: Noun plus -eul, then wihayeo, then drink.

words.note: The turn of the year, said at both new years Korea keeps. It opens the greeting and never moves from the front of it.
The luck the listener is told to receive. In this greeting it carries no particle at all, which is part of what makes the phrase fixed.

sentences.trap: English wishes the year to you; Korean tells you to receive the luck. The verb is the listener's, which is why it is badeuseyo and never a form of to be.

variations.changed: the greeting with the year left off, usable any time
the greeting with its ordinary answer beside it

mistake.why: This reports that there is a lot of luck in the new year. The greeting is an instruction to the listener to receive it, and it is said whole or not at all.

sentences.usage: The first thing said to anybody, for the whole first week of the year.
sentences.mnemonic: Receive the luck — do not wish it.

words.note: Opens the condolence and appears almost nowhere else. It is not an adverb a learner can move or reuse; it belongs to this sentence.
The person who has died, named with distance rather than by name. -ui is the of that ties them to what follows.
What the sentence prays for. It exists in this formula and hardly anywhere else, which is why the phrase is learned whole.
The deferential form of to pray. It closes the condolence and is not a verb to build other sentences with.

sentences.trap: There is nothing to improvise here. The English instinct is to add — I cannot imagine, tell me if I can help — and every addition makes it worse. Say it once, briefly, and stop.

variations.changed: samga dropped, which is the only piece that ever is

variations.display: Samga goin-ui myeongbog-eul bimnida. Sangsim-i keusigetseumnida.
variations.script: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다. 상심이 크시겠습니다.
variations.cue: My sincere condolences. This must be a great grief.
variations.changed: the second formula added, which is as long as it goes

mistake.why: Both sentences are correct Korean and neither belongs at a funeral. An improvised condolence puts the speaker's feeling in the room; the formula keeps it out, and that is the point of having one.

sentences.usage: Said once, at the door of the funeral hall, and then not repeated.
sentences.mnemonic: Four words, in that order, every time.

sentences.cue: This must be a great grief for you.

words.note: The bereaved person's grief, named rather than asked about. It is the subject of the sentence, so the speaker never says I about it.
Big, with the honorific for the listener and the ending that guesses rather than claims. Learned inside this formula, not as a verb to reuse.

sentences.trap: Korean guesses at another person's feeling and never asserts it. The ending is what does that, and dropping it turns a condolence into a claim about somebody else's heart.

variations.changed: the other formula, said to the same person on the same day

variations.cue: This must be a great grief. Thank you.
variations.changed: the exchange as it actually runs, both halves short

mistake.why: The register has collapsed and the guess has become a statement. Said to a bereaved person it tells them how they feel, in the voice you would use about the weather.

sentences.usage: To the family, standing, immediately after the bow.
sentences.mnemonic: Guess at the grief; never announce it.

sentences.cue: At a funeral that is what you say.

words.note: The occasion that owns the condolence. -eseo-neun sets it against every other occasion, which is exactly what this sentence is doing.
L5-M1's malhaeyo in the register this module produces. Same verb, same meaning; only the ending has moved.

sentences.trap: geureoke here points at the whole recited formula, not at a manner. The sentence is not about how to sound; it is about which words to use.

variations.cue: I am going to a funeral.
variations.changed: the plain locative, and the occasion as a destination

variations.cue: At a funeral that is what you say.
variations.changed: the -yo register, explaining it to a friend rather than in the room

mistake.why: Two endings on one verb. -(seu)pnida attaches to the stem, so a finished -yo form cannot carry it: the choice is malhaeyo or malhamnida, never both.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody who has never been what will be expected of them.

words.note: Everybody who came rather than everybody who is hosting. In front of yeoreobun it is how a host opens an address to the room.
The stem shape that jusipsio and juseyo both attach to. On its own it is not a finished sentence and never stands alone.
L1-M3's juseyo raised to the register a room asks for. It asks a hall; juseyo asks a person, and nothing else about the request changes.

sentences.trap: This is a host's line, not an announcement. L4-M7 owns the station and the intercom; here the same register is being spoken by somebody standing in the room.

variations.changed: the request without the address
juseyo for jusipsio: one person instead of a room

mistake.why: A finished verb cannot take jusipsio. The request rides on the -eo stem, gidaryeo, and stacking a second ending in front of it leaves two verbs where there should be one.

sentences.usage: A host at a wedding hall, holding a room while something is set up.
sentences.mnemonic: Stem plus jusipsio: asking a room.

sentences.cue: Excuse me. I will give the congratulatory address.

words.note: Said before taking a room's attention or crossing in front of people. It apologises for the interruption, not for a wrong.
The short speech given at a wedding or an opening. It is an occasion's own word, and it names the slot rather than the words in it.

sentences.trap: sillyehamnida is not joesonghamnida. L2-M1's word apologises for something done; this one asks permission for something about to be done, and a funeral takes neither.

variations.changed: the interruption alone

variations.cue: I will give the congratulatory address.
variations.changed: the announcement with no apology in front of it

mistake.why: joesonghamnida apologises for a fault. Opening a wedding speech with it says something has gone wrong, when all you are doing is asking for the room.

sentences.usage: Stepping up to the microphone at a wedding.
sentences.mnemonic: Sillye asks for the floor; joesong admits a fault.

words.note: The welcome a host gives a room at the start of an occasion. Said to the whole room at once, never to one arriving guest at a door.

sentences.trap: Not the shopkeeper's welcome. That one is a different phrase built on L1-M9's eoseo, and using this one at a doorway sounds like an opening ceremony for a single customer.

variations.changed: the welcome without the address
the whole of a short opening, which is two sentences

mistake.why: jusipsio makes a request, and a welcome asks for nothing. The greeting is finished as it stands; adding the request form asks the guests to welcome themselves.

sentences.usage: First words from the front of the room, before anything else happens.
sentences.mnemonic: Welcome the room, not the door.

words.note: The word Korean reaches for where English would say my — my company, my family. In a toast it is who the glass is being raised for.

sentences.trap: The frame runs either way round: geonbae first, or the noun first and geonbae as the last word. What it never does is grow a sentence in the middle.

variations.changed: the frame alone, with the shout left off
the shortest toast a host can give

mistake.display: Yeoreobun, uri-reul wihayeo, oneul jeongmal gamsahamnida, geonbae!
mistake.script: 여러분, 우리를 위하여, 오늘 정말 감사합니다, 건배!
mistake.why: Every word is right and it is no longer a toast. A Korean toast is a word with a noun in front of it; a thank-you in the middle turns it into the speech L5-M6 will teach.

sentences.usage: Standing, glass up, at the end of the meal rather than the start of a story.
sentences.mnemonic: A noun, wihayeo, geonbae — and stop.

comprehensionPool.cue: This must be a great grief for you.
At a funeral that is what you say.
I will give the congratulatory address.
